content: Atriplex is a genus of plants that includes between 100 and 200 species, commonly referred to as saltbush or orache. These plants are highly adaptable and can be found in a variety of environments, including deserts, seashores, and areas with high soil salinity. They are also capable of thriving in moist conditions. Atriplex belongs to the goosefoot subfamily (Chenopodioideae) within the Amaranthaceae family, as classified by the APG II system. Historically, this subfamily was considered a separate family known as Chenopodiaceae. The name Atriplex originates from Latin and was used by Pliny the Elder to describe edible oraches. Saltbush plants are particularly notable for their ability to tolerate and retain high levels of salt in their leaves. This characteristic makes them valuable in regions affected by soil salination. Additionally, Atriplex species serve as food sources for the larvae of certain Lepidoptera species and provide shelter and hunting grounds for spiders like Phidippus californicus and other arthropods in otherwise barren habitats. Many Atriplex species are edible, with the Garden Orache (Atriplex hortensis) being the most commonly consumed by humans. The use of Atriplex as a food source dates back to at least the late Epipaleolithic or Mesolithic periods. For example, the Ertebølle culture likely used Common Orache (Atriplex patula) as a vegetable. In the biblical Book of Job, the term mallûḥa (מַלּ֣וּחַ), which likely refers to Mediterranean Saltbush (Atriplex halimus), is mentioned as a food consumed by social outcasts. In Australia, Grey Saltbush (Atriplex cinerea) has been used as bushfood since prehistoric times. Native Americans consumed Chamiso (Atriplex canescens) and Shadscale (Atriplex confertifolia), while Spearscale (Atriplex hastata) was a food source in rural Eurasia. The Garden Orache (Atriplex hortensis), also known as Red Orach, Mountain Spinach, or French Spinach, is an annual leafy vegetable with a salty, spinach-like flavor. It can grow to a height of 1–2 meters (3–6 feet), and its leaves are used either cooked or raw in salads. Historically, it was widely cultivated in Mediterranean regions until spinach became the preferred leafy vegetable. The leaves of Garden Orache come in red, white, and green varieties. In Italy, the green leaves were once used to color pasta. Additionally, orach leaves are sometimes used to balance the acidic flavor of sorrel in culinary applications. Meat from sheep that graze on saltbush has been found to contain surprisingly high levels of vitamin E. This meat is leaner, more hydrated, and has consumer appeal comparable to grain-fed lamb. The elevated vitamin E levels may provide health benefits to the animals while also extending the shelf life and preserving the fresh red color of the meat. This effect has been observed in sheep grazing on Old Man Saltbush (Atriplex nummularia) and River Saltbush (Atriplex amnicola). Interestingly, sheep appear to prefer the more fibrous but less nutritious River Saltbush for reasons that remain unclear. Saltbushes are also used in landscaping as ornamental plants and for preventing soil erosion in coastal areas. Old Man Saltbush has been successfully employed in the rehabilitation of old mining sites, such as those around Lightning Ridge in Australia. The genus Atriplex includes a wide variety of species, such as Maritime Saltbush (Atriplex acadiensis), Alaska Orache (Atriplex alaskensis), Mediterranean Saltbush (Atriplex halimus), and Old Man Saltbush (Atriplex nummularia), among many others. Some species formerly classified under Atriplex, such as Chenopodium album and Halimione portulacoides, have since been reclassified into other genera.
